Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a faithfully flat ring map $A\to B$, base change identifies $A$-modules with $B$-modules equipped with a descent isomorphism between their two pullbacks to $B\otimes_AB$, satisfying the cocycle identity over the triple tensor product. The same is true for commutative unital algebras, when transport is an algebra isomorphism. Writing transport as $\theta:N\otimes_AB\to B\otimes_AN$, the descended module or algebra is
$$D=\{n\in N:\theta(n\otimes1)=1\otimes n\},$$
and $B\otimes_AD\to N$, $b\otimes d\mapsto bd$, is an isomorphism respecting the datum.

derivations.claim: Let \(T\to[X/G]\) correspond to a left torsor \(P\to T\) and an equivariant map \(\phi:P\to X\). An object of \(X\times_{[X/G]}T\) is a point \(x\in X\) and an equivariant isomorphism from the trivial left torsor to \(P\), compatible with \(\phi\). Such an isomorphism is determined by the image \(p\in P\) of the identity, and sends \(g\) to \(g p\); the compatibility condition forces \(x=\phi(p)\). Thus \(X\times_{[X/G]}T\cong P\). Since \(P\to T\) is a torsor, it is a smooth surjective scheme morphism by [F3] and the local triviality in [F1]. Hence \(X\to[X/G]\) is a representable smooth surjective atlas.

For two objects \((P,\phi)\) and \((P',\phi')\) over a scheme \(T\), their isomorphism functor is the subfunctor of \(\operatorname{Isom}_G(P,P')\) on which \(\phi'\circ f=\phi\). After a common fppf cover trivializing both torsors, and after restricting to affine opens of the cover, \(\operatorname{Isom}_G(P,P')\cong G\times T\). With the chosen trivializing sections \(p,p'\), the condition is the inverse image of the diagonal \(X\hookrightarrow X\times X\) under the two evaluation maps \(f\mapsto(\phi'(f(p)),\phi(p))\). The diagonal of affine \(X\) is closed, so this is a closed subscheme of \(G\times T\), affine over \(T\). The isomorphism functor therefore has affine local representatives with their canonical descent data; [F4] makes this affine descent datum effective. Thus the isomorphism functor is represented by an affine scheme over \(T\), which proves the diagonal is affine, hence representable.

By steps 1.1 and 1.2, the quotient stack has a smooth surjective representable atlas and representable diagonal. These are exactly the two conditions in [F2], so \([X/G]\) is an algebraic stack. The inherited AC appears only in [A1] through those defining suppliers.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let \(X\) be an affine finite-type
\(\mathbb C\)-scheme with an algebraic action of
\(G=\prod_{r=1}^m\operatorname{GL}_{n_r,\mathbb C}\), allowing \(n_r=0\).
Then the quotient stack \([X/G]\), defined by \(G\)-torsors with equivariant
maps to \(X\), is an algebraic stack. The morphism \(X\to[X/G]\) from the
trivial torsor is a smooth surjective representable atlas, and the diagonal
of \([X/G]\) is representable by affine schemes.

Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over $k$. For $0\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ denotes the parameter set of $r$-dimensional linear subspaces of $V$. Thus $\operatorname{Gr}(0,V)=\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}(n,V)=\{V\}$. For $r<0$ or $r>n$ we set $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)=\varnothing$.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space of dimension $n\ge1$. The set $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$ of complete flags
$$0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\dots\subset V_n=V,\qquad \dim V_i=i,$$
carries the structure of a smooth projective classical $k$-variety: it is the closed subvariety of the product of Grassmannians $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbf{Gr}_i(V)$ cut out by the incidence conditions $V_i\subseteq V_{i+1}$, embedded in a product of projective spaces by Plücker coordinates. The group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ acts transitively on $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$, the stabilizer of a flag is a closed subgroup scheme of $\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and the stabilizer of a complete flag is solvable.

Assume AC. Every separated finite-type group scheme over a characteristic-zero field is smooth. No affineness, reducedness, or connectedness assumption is required.

**Definition.** The **projective bundle** of $E$ over $S$ is the relative Proj
$$\pi:\mathbb P_S(E)=\operatorname{Proj}_S\operatorname{Sym}(E)\longrightarrow S,$$
with the relative twists $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_S(E)}(n)$, $n\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-relative-proj-quasi-coherent-graded-algebra]]). Since
$\operatorname{Sym}(E)$ is generated in degree one, the degree-one part
$\operatorname{Sym}^1(E)=E$ generates the whole algebra, and there is a
canonical surjection
$$\pi^*E\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_S(E)}(1),$$
the **tautological quotient** of the pullback of $E$; it is locally given by
the coordinate sections of a projective space, over an open set on which
$E\cong\mathcal O_S^{\,r}$.

A **1-morphism of stacks in groupoids**
$f\colon\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ over $(\mathit{Sch}/S)_{fppf}$
([[def-descent-data-and-stack-in-groupoids]]) is **representable by algebraic
spaces** when for every $S$-scheme $T$ and every 1-morphism
$T\to\mathcal Y$ — equivalently, by the 2-Yoneda lemma, for every object
$x\in\mathcal Y_T$ — the 2-fibre product
$\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y,T}$ is equivalent to the stack in setoids
$\mathcal S_Z$ of an algebraic space $Z$ over $T$. Smooth, etale, surjective
and other fibrewise properties are then defined by base change to schemes, so
the definition specializes to the presheaf case when $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$
are stacks in setoids of presheaves of sets.

A morphism of schemes $f:X\to S$ is **proper** if and only if it is separated,
of finite type, and universally closed. Here separatedness has the meaning of
[[def-separated-morphism-schemes]], finite type has the meaning of
[[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]], and universally closed
has the meaning of [[def-universally-closed-morphism]]. The definition applies
to arbitrary schemes: it assumes neither Noetherian hypotheses nor finite
presentation.

derivations.claim: For each arrow \(h:i\to j\), the free off-diagonal block in \(\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}(V_i^{\mathbf b},V_j^{\mathbf a})\); hence \(\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\to \operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf a)\times\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf b)\) is a vector bundle of rank \(e=\sum_{h:i\to j}b_i a_j\). The block-parabolic group \(P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\) maps onto its block-diagonal Levi group \(L=G_{\mathbf a}\times G_{\mathbf b}\); its kernel \(U\) consists of upper-right vertex blocks and is the vector group of dimension \(u=\sum_i a_i b_i\).

Let an arbitrary scheme \(T\) map to \(\mathfrak M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\). By the quotient-stack definition this is a family of vector bundles \(E_i\) of ranks \(a_i+b_i\), with arrow maps. The base change of \(p\) parametrizes subbundles \(F_i\subset E_i\) of ranks \(a_i\) preserved by every arrow. It is the closed subscheme of the relative Grassmannian \(\prod_i\operatorname{Gr}_T(a_i,E_i)\) cut out by the vanishing of the bundle maps \(F_i\to E_j\to E_j/F_j\) for each arrow \(h:i\to j\). Each relative Grassmannian is a closed subscheme of \(\mathbb P_T(\bigwedge^{a_i}E_i)\) by the relative Plucker map; on local frames this is the closed Plucker embedding of [F3], and the equations glue under changes of frame. Each such projective bundle is proper: after any base change \(T'\to T\), trivialize \(E_i\) over an open cover of \(T'\); on each open the projection is a projective-space projection, hence proper by [F4]. The image of a closed set is closed on each member of the cover and therefore closed globally; separatedness and finite type are also local on the base. Thus every base change is proper by [F7]. The product of these proper maps is proper by base change and composition [F4]. The arrow conditions are closed because they are zero loci of regular bundle maps, so the incidence scheme is proper over \(T\) as a closed subscheme of that product [F4]. In the standard frame atlas this scheme is exactly \[ I_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}= \{(X,(F_i)):\dim F_i=a_i,\ X_h(F_i)\subseteq F_j \text{ for every }h:i\to j\}. \], and its defining equations are the same zero-locus equations just described; in an ordinary Grassmannian chart they are the vanishing of the complementary matrix block. Hence every scheme base change of \(p\) is a proper scheme.

Pull back \(q\) along the atlas \(Z=\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf a)\times\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf b) \to\mathfrak M_{\mathbf a}\times\mathfrak M_{\mathbf b}\). This fixes the endpoint representations. Every middle representation is a block matrix from step 1.1, and every isomorphism inducing the identity on the fixed endpoints is a unique upper-right vertex block. Hence the pullback stack is \([Y/U]\to Z\), where \(Y\to Z\) is the rank-\(e\) vector bundle of off-diagonal blocks and \(U\) is the rank-\(u\) vector group of changes of splitting. The atlas \(Y\to[Y/U]\) is a smooth \(U\)-torsor; its composite \(Y\to Z\) is a vector bundle projection of relative dimension \(e\). By the atlas convention just stated, \([Y/U]\to Z\) is smooth of relative stack dimension \(e-u\). Smoothness and relative dimension are checked after the displayed smooth target atlas, so the same holds for \(q\). Substitution of the definition of \(\chi_Q\) gives \(e-u=-\chi_Q(\mathbf b,\mathbf a)\), including arrows that are loops or occur with multiplicity.

The construction in step 1.2 identifies every scheme base change of \(p\) with the incidence scheme, so [F7] proves that \(p\) is representable by schemes, hence by algebraic spaces; the same step proves every such base-changed map is proper. If some \(a_i=0\) or \(a_i=a_i+b_i\), the corresponding Grassmannian is a point and the same closed-incidence argument applies. Step 2.1 proves the smoothness of \(q\), so both claims of the Statement follow. AC is used only through [A1].

Assume AC as inherited from the equivariant constructible category. Let \(Q\)
be a finite quiver. A **quiver potential** is a finite
\(\mathbb C\)-linear combination of directed cycles in the path algebra
\(\mathbb C Q=\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb ZQ\), modulo cyclic
rotation of each cycle. For a cycle
\(h_1:i_0\to i_1,\ldots,h_\ell:i_{\ell-1}\to i_0\) and a representation
\(X\in\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf d)\), its trace is
\[
\operatorname{tr}(X_{h_\ell}\cdots X_{h_1}).
\]
Extending linearly defines the regular function \(W_{\mathbf d}\) on
\(\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf d)\). Its basis invariance and additivity on
extensions are proved in
[[lem-quiver-potential-trace-is-additive-on-extensions]], and
\(\operatorname{Crit}(W_{\mathbf d})\) denotes its critical locus, the zero
scheme of the differential \(dW_{\mathbf d}\).

derivations.claim: For a cycle \(h_1,\ldots,h_\ell\), the product \(X_{h_\ell}\cdots X_{h_1}\) is block upper triangular because products of block-upper-triangular matrices remain block upper triangular. Its two diagonal blocks are respectively the cycle products on \(M_{\mathbf a}\) and \(M_{\mathbf b}\): this follows inductively from \(\operatorname{diag}(AB)=\operatorname{diag}(A)\operatorname{diag}(B)\) for two block-upper-triangular matrices \(A,B\).

The trace of a block-upper-triangular matrix is the sum of the traces of its diagonal blocks. Therefore the trace of this cycle on \(M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\) is the sum of its traces on \(M_{\mathbf a}\) and \(M_{\mathbf b}\).

A change of basis conjugates the matrix product of a cycle, and trace is invariant under conjugation; cyclic rotation also preserves trace since \(\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\). Applying step 2.1 to each cycle and summing its coefficient in \(W\) proves the displayed identity and the basis invariance of \(W_{\mathbf d}\).

derivations.claim: For dimension vectors \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c\), the left parenthesization first chooses an exact sequence \(0\to M_{\mathbf a}\to M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\to M_{\mathbf b}\to0\) and then an exact sequence \(0\to M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\to M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c} \to M_{\mathbf c}\to0\). The resulting data are exactly a flag \(0\subset M_{\mathbf a}\subset M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b} \subset M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c}\) whose successive quotients have dimensions \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c\), in that order. Pullback to the stack of these flags identifies the composite pullback and pushforward with the two maps in the left-associated convolution.

If either dimension vector is \(\mathbf 0\), the corresponding exact sequence has a unique zero subobject or a unique zero quotient. Hence both maps in the correspondence reduce to the identity on \(\mathfrak M_{\mathbf d}\); the class \(1\) acts as the identity on either side.

In the right parenthesization, the first exact sequence is \(0\to M_{\mathbf b}\to M_{\mathbf b+\mathbf c}\to M_{\mathbf c}\to0\); pulling its subobject back along the quotient \(M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c}\to M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c}/M_{\mathbf a}\) gives the unique intermediate subobject \(M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\). Conversely quotienting the two-step flag of step 1.1 by \(M_{\mathbf a}\) recovers that sequence. Thus the right composite uses the same flag stack. The Cartesian base-change and composition identities in [F3] make the two induced homology maps equal.

The degree shifts agree: bilinearity of \(\chi_Q\) gives \[ -\chi_Q(\mathbf b,\mathbf a) -\chi_Q(\mathbf c,\mathbf a+\mathbf b) =-\chi_Q(\mathbf c,\mathbf b) -\chi_Q(\mathbf b+\mathbf c,\mathbf a). \] So the equality in step 2.1 is an equality in the same graded component.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 show that the two parenthesizations agree in the same graded component, while step 1.2 supplies a two-sided unit. Bilinearity extends these identities to the direct sum \(\mathcal H_Q\). AC is used only through [A1].

Assume AC as inherited from the equivariant constructible category. Let \(Q\)
be a finite quiver. A **quiver potential** is a finite
\(\mathbb C\)-linear combination of directed cycles in the path algebra
\(\mathbb C Q=\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb ZQ\), modulo cyclic
rotation of each cycle. For a cycle
\(h_1:i_0\to i_1,\ldots,h_\ell:i_{\ell-1}\to i_0\) and a representation
\(X\in\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf d)\), its trace is
\[
\operatorname{tr}(X_{h_\ell}\cdots X_{h_1}).
\]
Extending linearly defines the regular function \(W_{\mathbf d}\) on
\(\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf d)\). Its basis invariance and additivity on
extensions are proved in
[[lem-quiver-potential-trace-is-additive-on-extensions]], and
\(\operatorname{Crit}(W_{\mathbf d})\) denotes its critical locus, the zero
scheme of the differential \(dW_{\mathbf d}\).

Let \(W\) be a potential of a finite quiver \(Q\), and let
\(0\to M_{\mathbf a}\to M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\to M_{\mathbf b}\to0\)
be represented by a point of the exact-sequence stack. Then
\[
W_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}(M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b})
=W_{\mathbf a}(M_{\mathbf a})+W_{\mathbf b}(M_{\mathbf b}).
\]
In particular, \(W_{\mathbf d}\) is invariant under change of basis.

Assume AC. Let \(Q\) be a finite quiver and let \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\) be
dimension vectors. In the notation of
[[def-quiver-representation-stacks-and-exact-sequence-correspondences]], the
map \(q:\mathfrak E_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\to
\mathfrak M_{\mathbf a}\times\mathfrak M_{\mathbf b}\) is a smooth morphism of
algebraic stacks of relative complex dimension
\[
r_Q(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)
=\sum_{h:i\to j} b_i a_j-\sum_{i\in Q_0}a_i b_i
=-\chi_Q(\mathbf b,\mathbf a),
\]
where
\[
\chi_Q(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)
=\sum_i u_i v_i-\sum_{h:i\to j}u_i v_j.
\]
The forgetful map \(p:\mathfrak E_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\to
\mathfrak M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}\) is representable and proper. These claims
allow loops, multiple arrows, zero coordinates, and the empty quiver.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

derivations.claim: For any split \(\mathbf d=\mathbf a+\mathbf b\), [F2] identifies the potential on the extension correspondence with the sum of the two diagonal potentials. The Thom–Sebastiani map in [F1] therefore identifies the coefficient on that correspondence with the external product of the \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) coefficients at values \(z_1,z_2\), in output value \(z_1+z_2\). The proper push and smooth pull in [F1] and [F3] consequently define the product of every pair of homogeneous summands.
In dimension zero, the supplied coefficient is \(\mathbb Q\) with its identity class; the zero-subobject and whole-subobject correspondences are identity maps. Hence this class is a two-sided unit.

For three dimension vectors, an iterated product in either parenthesization is represented by the same flag of subrepresentations \(0\subset M_{\mathbf a}\subset M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b} \subset M_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c}\). Additivity in [F2] identifies the potential there with \(W_{\mathbf a}\boxplus W_{\mathbf b}\boxplus W_{\mathbf c}\), and the associative external-product identification in [F1] gives the same coefficient in either order. The Cartesian base-change and composition identities in [F1] therefore identify the two induced pull-push maps.

The shifts agree because \[ -\chi_Q(\mathbf b,\mathbf a) -\chi_Q(\mathbf c,\mathbf a+\mathbf b) =-\chi_Q(\mathbf c,\mathbf b) -\chi_Q(\mathbf b+\mathbf c,\mathbf a), \] by bilinearity of \(\chi_Q\). Thus the maps of step 2.1 land in the same graded component.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove associativity in the same graded component, and step 1.2 proves unitality for the conditional construction. No property of a canonical vanishing-cycle realization beyond the explicit hypotheses [F1] is used. AC is inherited through [A1].

Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over $k$. For $0\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ denotes the parameter set of $r$-dimensional linear subspaces of $V$. Thus $\operatorname{Gr}(0,V)=\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}(n,V)=\{V\}$. For $r<0$ or $r>n$ we set $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)=\varnothing$.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space of dimension $n\ge1$. The set $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$ of complete flags
$$0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\dots\subset V_n=V,\qquad \dim V_i=i,$$
carries the structure of a smooth projective classical $k$-variety: it is the closed subvariety of the product of Grassmannians $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbf{Gr}_i(V)$ cut out by the incidence conditions $V_i\subseteq V_{i+1}$, embedded in a product of projective spaces by Plücker coordinates. The group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ acts transitively on $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$, the stabilizer of a flag is a closed subgroup scheme of $\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and the stabilizer of a complete flag is solvable.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

derivations.claim: A one-loop representation of dimension one is a scalar, and change of basis by \(\operatorname{GL}_1\) fixes it because conjugation by a scalar is trivial. A dimension-two representation is a \(2\times2\) matrix with conjugation action. Preserving a chosen line makes the matrix upper triangular in an adapted basis, as displayed.

For this quiver the off-diagonal rank is \(e=1\) and the unipotent vertex-block rank is \(u=1\); hence \(q\) has relative stack dimension \(e-u=0\), agreeing with \(-\chi_Q(1,1)=0\). For the splitting change represented by \(t\in\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb C,\mathbb C)\), the change-of-basis matrix \(g_t=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}\) acts by \(A\mapsto g_tAg_t^{-1}\), sending \(c\) to \(c+(\mu-\lambda)t\). Thus when \(\lambda\ne\mu\) the extension coordinate is removed by a unique splitting change, whereas when \(\lambda=\mu\) it is unchanged; this is consistent with a zero-dimensional stack morphism, not a claim that all extension fibers are points.

The fiber of \(p\) at a scalar matrix \(\lambda I\) is all of \(\mathbb P^1\), so it is positive-dimensional. For a diagonal matrix with distinct eigenvalues, an invariant line must be an eigenspace, giving exactly two points. For a non-scalar Jordan matrix \(\lambda I+N\) with \(N^2=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}N=1\), an invariant line is \(N\)-stable; the nilpotent map induced on a one-dimensional line is zero, so the line lies in \(\ker N\), which is the unique invariant line. These fibers agree with the closed incidence projection to \(\operatorname{Mat}_2(\mathbb C)\times\mathbb P^1\) and do not affect properness.

The incidence equations \(A(L)\subseteq L\) are closed in \(\operatorname{Mat}_2(\mathbb C)\times\mathbb P^1\), so the forgetful map \(p\) is projective and proper by [F2]. The example includes a loop and checks why stack-relative dimension and properness must be read from the specified correspondence, not from finiteness of its fibers. AC is inherited through [A1].

derivations.claim: The trace definition in [F1] gives \(W_1(z)=z^2\). Its differential is \(dW_1=2z\,dz\); since the coefficient field has characteristic zero, this vanishes exactly at \(z=0\), where \(W_1(0)=0\). Thus the critical locus and critical value are as stated.

For any sufficiently small \(\epsilon\ne0\), the local Milnor fiber \(z^2=\epsilon\) in a disk about zero consists of the two distinct points \(\sqrt\epsilon\) and \(-\sqrt\epsilon\). Its reduced zeroth cohomology is \(\mathbb Q\), generated by the difference of the two point classes. When \(\epsilon\) goes once around zero, the two roots exchange, so this generator maps to its negative. The on-shell coefficient at this critical point is therefore one-dimensional with monodromy \(-1\), in the stated convention.

This calculation identifies the local critical datum for \(W=x^2\); it does not establish the existence of the full equivariant Thom–Sebastiani/proper-pushforward package or an associative critical CoHA. Those are the explicit additional inputs in [[def-critical-quiver-coha-from-vanishing-cycle-data]] and are recorded as unresolved for the standard realization.
